title: Hummus vs. tahini: nutrition differences

seo.title: Hummus vs. tahini: nutrition differences
seo.meta_description: Tahini is far more concentrated than hummus. Compare equal 30 g servings for calories, protein, fat, fiber and minerals.
seo.search_intent: Compare hummus and tahini nutrition using equal serving weights

excerpt: Hummus and tahini are not interchangeable foods: tahini is concentrated sesame paste and is often one ingredient in hummus. In equal 30 g servings, the USDA references used here provide about 73 calories, 2.2 g protein, 5.1 g fat and 1.6 g fiber for hummus, versus about 209 calories, 5.9 g protein, 18.7 g fat and 2.5 g fiber for tahini.
content_html:
Hummus and tahini sit next to each other so often that they can look like two versions of the same dip. They are not. Tahini is ground sesame, while hummus usually combines tahini with chickpeas, water or lemon, and other ingredients. That difference explains why equal spoonfuls can have very different calorie and nutrient concentrations.

Hummus spreads the sesame paste across a wetter legume-based mixture. Tahini keeps the concentrated composition of sesame seeds. Neither is automatically the better food; they simply do different jobs and deliver different amounts of energy and nutrients at the same weight.

Equal weights make the contrast clear

Using two USDA reference foods, a 30-gram comparison looks like this:

Per 30 gPlain hummusTahini
Calories~73~209
Protein~2.2 g~5.9 g
Fat~5.1 g~18.7 g
Fiber~1.6 g~2.5 g
Carbohydrate~4.5 g~4.3 g

Tahini has almost three times the calories at the same weight because sesame paste is much richer in fat. That is not a nutritional flaw. It means a tablespoon of tahini should not be interpreted like a tablespoon of hummus, especially when you are comparing energy density.

Thirty grams of hummus can be a visible portion of dip. The same weight of tahini is often used as a concentrated ingredient and thinned with lemon juice, water, yogurt, or other ingredients before serving. Equal-weight data explain concentration; normal serving patterns explain how that concentration plays out in an actual meal.

Why tahini provides more protein and minerals per gram

The tahini reference contains about 19.7 grams of protein, 357 milligrams of magnesium, and 7 milligrams of iron per 100 grams. Hummus, because sesame and chickpeas are mixed with wetter ingredients, comes in at about 7.3 grams of protein per 100 grams and is less mineral-dense by weight.

Thirty grams of tahini therefore provides roughly 107 milligrams of magnesium and 2.1 milligrams of iron. Those figures are useful reference points, but individual products vary. Sesame variety, whether the seeds are hulled, and processing can affect mineral content, especially calcium. Numbers for whole sesame seeds should not automatically be assigned to every jar of tahini.

Hummus offers a different advantage that is easy to miss when looking at one mineral at a time: it combines legumes and sesame in a wetter food that can be eaten in a larger portion for fewer calories. Store-bought hummus can also vary widely in sodium and added oil, so the Nutrition Facts panel is worth checking when those details matter to you.

Hummus gives you more volume for fewer calories

A 60-gram serving of the plain hummus reference works out to roughly 146 calories, 4.4 grams of protein, and 3.2 grams of fiber. Sixty grams of the tahini reference would exceed 400 calories. Tahini is usually served in smaller amounts precisely because it is so concentrated and because its sesame flavor is strong.

That volume difference can matter in a meal. Hummus can cover a larger area of a sandwich, accompany raw vegetables, or serve as a substantial dip without making the sauce the most energy-dense part of the plate. A spoonful or two of tahini can flavor an entire bowl or dressing, but free-pouring it changes calories quickly.

Recipes add another layer of variation. Hummus made with generous olive oil can be substantially richer than a leaner version. Tahini whisked with water and lemon becomes a much larger amount of sauce, but the calories still come from however much tahini went into the mixture. Comparing the finished serving is more informative than comparing recipe names.

Which one makes more sense?

They play different roles. Hummus works as a larger dip, spread, or meal component that combines chickpeas, sesame, and plant fat. Tahini works especially well as a smaller, concentrated ingredient in dressings, sauces, desserts, and hummus itself.

If your priority is protein or magnesium per gram, tahini is more concentrated. If you want more volume for fewer calories per spoonful, hummus generally fits better. If total protein is the main goal, though, neither necessarily replaces a clear serving of beans, fish, poultry, eggs, dairy, tofu, or another protein-rich food; portion size still determines the contribution.

The useful question is not which one is healthier, but how much you are using and what job it has in the meal. Hummus and tahini can easily coexist: one as a larger chickpea-based preparation, the other as a dense sesame paste that contributes flavor, fat, and minerals.

faq.question: Which has more protein, hummus or tahini?
faq.answer: Tahini by weight: about 19.7 g/100 g versus 7.3 g/100 g in the hummus reference.

faq.question: Which has more calories?
faq.answer: Tahini clearly: about 697 calories/100 g versus 243 calories/100 g in the hummus reference.

faq.question: Is tahini an ingredient in hummus?
faq.answer: Yes. Classic hummus typically combines tahini with chickpeas, lemon, garlic and other ingredients depending on the recipe.

faq.question: Which has more fiber?
faq.answer: Per 100 g, the tahini reference has 8.4 g versus 5.4 g in hummus, although tahini is usually eaten in a smaller serving.
